The Imperative of Legal Mandates for Social Media Platforms to Host All Legal Content: A Defense of Absolute Free Speech and Common Carrier Principles

In a world where social media platforms have become the public squares of the 21st century, the question of whether these entities should be legally compelled to host all legal content—regardless of its societal acceptability—strikes at the heart of democratic values. Proponents of free expression argue that allowing platforms to act as arbitrary gatekeepers of discourse risks normalizing censorship, eroding the principle that governments, not private companies, should define the boundaries of acceptable speech. By legally requiring social media platforms to adopt common carrier obligations—treating users as neutral consumers of an essential service—society can ensure that free speech is shielded from corporate bias, ideological overreach, and the corrosive influence of public opinion. Such a mandate would enshrine absolute free speech as a cornerstone of digital communication while preventing the unchecked concentration of power in the hands of a few tech giants.

The Foundations of Absolute Free Speech

The concept of free speech, particularly encapsulated in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, has long been defended as a bulwark against tyranny. Its essence lies in the idea that truth emerges from the free exchange of ideas, even—and especially—when those ideas are unpopular. Justice Holmes’ argument in Whitney v. California (1925) that “the best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market” underscores the idea that ideas, however distasteful, should be allowed to exist so that society can collectively reject or refute them.

In the digital age, platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube have become the primary arenas for this “marketplace of ideas.” Yet these corporations increasingly exercise editorial control, unilaterally banning accounts, shadowbanning users, or suppressing content that conflicts with their corporate values or public relations strategies. For example, Facebook’s periodic bans of hashtag-backed activism, such as #ReplaceTheCEO during CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s congressional testimony, demonstrate how private policies can silence dissent. A legal requirement to host all lawful content would prevent such arbitrary suppression of speech, ensuring that platforms remain forums for open discourse rather than tools of corporate censorship.

Common Carrier Obligations: A Legal Framework for Equality

Common carrier laws have a long tradition in democratic societies. From railroads to telecommunication networks, these principles enshrine the obligation to serve all patrons without discrimination. A telephone company, for instance, cannot refuse service to a customer simply because its executives oppose their political views. By extending this logic to social media, platforms would be legally required to treat users as customers purchasing access to a communication medium—a tool, not a curated publication.

This framework is critical for preserving equity in speech. Without it, platforms wield disproportionate power to shape discourse, enabling them to promote or suppress voices based on ideological alignment. Companies might disproportionately target marginalized groups—such as activists, political minorities, or religious communities—with deplatforming campaigns to avoid backlash, financial loss, or regulatory scrutiny. Legally defining platforms as common carriers would prevent such power imbalances, just as it has long protected users of other essential services.

Addressing Critics: Harm, Definition, and the Slippery Slope

Opponents may argue that unchecked hate speech poses existential threats to vulnerable communities. While such concerns are valid, the alternative—granting platforms unchecked authority to police speech—is far more perilous. For instance, labeling climate change denial or progressive economic policies as “misinformation” could empower platforms to quash dissenting views. Legal mandates to host content would not excuse illegal activities such as threats of violence or incitement, which already fall outside protected speech. Platforms would still enforce laws against libel, defamation, or direct harm, but they could not act as “private sovereigns” policing ideological battles.

Moreover, the premise that platforms must moderate content to protect their own “brands” reflects a dangerous confluence of corporate self-interest and quasi-governmental authority. When Facebook appoints itself judge and jury of “acceptable” speech, it substitutes its leadership’s subjective values for the legal protections enshrined in democratic constitutions. This undermines the separation of powers and risks creating a chilling effect where users self-censor to avoid scrutiny.

An Ethical and Democratic Imperative

Adopting common carrier obligations for social media aligns with broader ethical imperatives. Digital platforms are not merely profit-driven enterprises; they are infrastructural arteries of modern society. From political mobilization to economic transactions, these platforms now underpin every facet of human life. When corporations claim the right to control speech, they position themselves as unelected guardians of societal norms—a role better reserved for transparent, accountable legal systems.

Furthermore, mandating neutrality would democratize discourse. Movements like the #MeToo campaign and the Arab Spring relied on social media’s capacity to amplify marginalized voices. Without the threat of arbitrary censorship, such movements could grow unimpeded. Conversely, if platforms retain unchecked power, their algorithms and moderation policies will increasingly dictate which ideas “qualify” for circulation—a paradoxical inversion where private entities, not citizens, determine the boundaries of public debate.

Conclusion

The erosion of free speech begins when gatekeepers are permitted to decide what ideas are “worth hearing.” By legislating social media platforms as common carriers obligated to host all legal content, society can firewall democratic discourse from corporate influence and ideological bias. This move would not glorify hate speech but instead place the responsibility for addressing harmful ideas squarely on the public as a whole—where robust debate, education, and counter-speech, rather than censorship, can win the day. In a world where technology increasingly shapes reality, ensuring neutrality in digital communication is not a radical notion—it is the only path to a free society.

Let us reimagine social media not as the opinionated publishers of today, but as the digital public squares of tomorrow: inclusive, unbiased, and true to the ideal that sunlight, not suppression, is the best disinfectant.

Legal and Structural Justifications

  1. Limiting Private Power

  • Targeted Regulation: Platforms could still enforce terms of service for non-legal issues (e.g., transactional fraud) without infringing on free speech.

Conclusion

Proponents argue that legally requiring platforms to host all legal content upholds free speech as a bedrock democratic value, prevents entrenched corporate control over discourse, and ensures that only democratically accountable authorities restrict expression. By treating legal content uniformly, the mandate fosters a more equitable and transparent digital landscape, aligning with foundational principles of rights protection and self-governance.

Introduction

In the marketplace of ideas, the freest societies thrive not by silencing dissent, but by amplifying every voice—no matter how repugnant. Anything less betrays democracy's core.

The Absolute Imperative of Free Speech

Free speech is not a polite suggestion; it is the oxygen of liberty. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes captured this in Abrams v. United States (1919): "The best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market." Absolute free speech means protecting even the most odious ideas, for only through exposure and refutation do they wither. Hate speech from groups like the Ku Klux Klan or neo-Nazis? Repulsive, yes—but legal under Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), which limits bans to imminent lawless action. Platforms have no right to preemptively bury it.

History vindicates this absolutism. The American Civil Liberties Union defended Nazis marching in Skokie, Illinois (1977), not out of sympathy, but because "counterspeech" is the antidote. John Stuart Mill echoed this in On Liberty (1859): silencing an opinion robs humanity of the chance to replace error with truth or refine truth through challenge. When platforms like Twitter banned President Trump in 2021 or YouTube demonetized PragerU for "controversial" views, they didn't eradicate hate—they drove it underground, fostering radicalization in unmoderated corners of the web.

Requiring platforms to host all legal content enforces this marketplace. Users decide what rises or falls via algorithms driven by engagement, not biased human moderators. This isn't anarchy; it's meritocracy of ideas, where the best speech prevails.

Platforms as Common Carriers: Historical and Legal Imperative

Social media are not quaint bookstores curating shelves; they are indispensable public utilities, the digital town squares where discourse happens. With billions of users, network effects create monopolies: Facebook controls 70% of U.S. social logins; Google owns 90% of search. They profit from Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996), which shields them from liability as "platforms," not "publishers." Yet when they moderate—like shadowbanning conservatives or purging "misinformation"—they become publishers, forfeiting that immunity (NetChoice v. Paxton, ongoing).

Enter common carrier doctrine: entities like AT&T or railroads must serve all customers without discrimination. Telegraphs faced this in the 19th century; the U.S. Supreme Court in Postal Telegraph-Cable Co. v. Adsit (1912) upheld non-discriminatory access. Why? Public necessity demands it—refusal to carry a message stifles commerce and speech.

Modern platforms fit perfectly. They transmit user-generated content via proprietary pipes, much like phone lines carry calls. In United States v. Manhattan Cable TV (1975), cable operators were deemed common carriers for public access channels. Social media demand the same: a "must-carry" rule for all legal speech. Legislation like the proposed Common Carrier Internet Transparency Act could mandate this, stripping editorial discretion while preserving Section 230 for pure transmission.

Opponents cry "private property!" But platforms aren't baking artisanal cakes; they're toll roads funded by public data and ad revenue. Their scale—global reach, algorithmic amplification—imposes common carrier duties, just as airlines can't refuse passengers based on politics.

Voluntary moderation is a farce. Platforms' "trust and safety" teams exhibit blatant bias: pre-2022 Twitter's File (revealed by Elon Musk) showed executives throttling right-wing voices while boosting leftists. Facebook's 2020 election meddling—censoring Hunter Biden stories—proved they tilt scales. Hate groups? Sure, they're booted, but so are feminists like J.K. Rowling for "transphobia" or COVID skeptics like Dr. Robert Malone.

This selective censorship breeds tyranny. Who defines "hate"? Yesterday's heretic is tomorrow's prophet—Galileo, MLK, suffragettes all faced "hate" labels. Platforms become Ministries of Truth, Orwellian arbiters wielding godlike power. Deplatforming Andrew Anglin's Daily Stormer in 2017 didn't erase neo-Nazism; it radicalized followers, arguably fueling events like Charlottesville.

Mandating all legal content ends this. Platforms focus on infrastructure, not ideology. Algorithms surface based on popularity, letting users mute or block individually. No more shadowbans; pure transparency.

Hate Speech: Protected, Not Privileged for Deletion

Hate groups test absolutism, but they prove its necessity. Legal speech—no threats, no incitement—must flow freely. The Westboro Baptist Church's "God Hates Fags" signs? Upheld in Snyder v. Phelps (2011). Platforms hosting Stormfront or Nation of Islam forums? Same logic. Exposure invites counterspeech: ADL fact-checks, SPLC exposes, users ratio-post mockery.

Economically, must-carry benefits all. Platforms grow via volume; niche hate content draws eyeballs (controversy = clicks). Advertisers fleeing? Let markets decide—users can boycott.

Conclusion: Reclaim the Republic of Letters

Requiring social media to host all legal content isn't optional—it's the bulwark against digital despotism. Grounded in absolute free speech, where ideas duel unrigged, and common carrier law, where monopolies serve indifferently, this policy restores the public square. Modern social media platforms, app stores, payment processors, web hosts, search engines, and other online intermediaries have become essential infrastructure for public communication. Popular speech does not need protection; unpopular speech does.

The central principle should be simple: if content is legal to publish, it should be legal to host. Platforms should be permitted—and required—to remove material that is unlawful, such as genuine threats, direct incitement under applicable law, fraud, child sexual abuse material, unlawful harassment, copyright infringement, and other clearly illegal content. But they should not be allowed to impose their own shifting ideological standards to silence lawful political, religious, cultural, or social views merely because those views offend employees, advertisers, activists, or influential users.

Absolute commitment to lawful speech is especially important when the speaker is hateful or extremist. The temptation to make exceptions for repugnant views is understandable. Yet every expansion of censorship power creates a precedent that can later be turned against dissidents, minorities, whistleblowers, journalists, labor organizers, religious groups, or ordinary citizens. A rule allowing platforms to remove “hate,” “misinformation,” “offensive content,” or “harmful ideas” is only as safe as the people defining those terms at a given moment. Such categories are often vague, politically contested, and susceptible to abuse.

History offers ample reason for caution. Governments and powerful institutions have routinely labeled dissenting ideas as dangerous, immoral, subversive, hateful, or false. Antiwar activists, civil-rights advocates, religious minorities, labor movements, LGBTQ advocates, and political reformers have all at times faced suppression in the name of public order or social harmony. A system built to silence today’s extremists may tomorrow be used to silence those challenging the powerful. The most durable protection against that danger is a bright-line rule: lawful speech must remain available for lawful distribution.

This approach is also consistent with the traditional common-carrier principle. Common carriers—such as telephone companies, postal services, railroads, and utilities—provide essential services to the public without discriminating based on viewpoint. A telephone company may not disconnect a customer because it disapproves of that customer’s politics. The postal service does not open letters and refuse delivery because the sender holds offensive beliefs. The operator of a road does not decide which political marchers may travel on it. These institutions may enforce neutral rules concerning payment, safety, technical capacity, and illegal activity, but they do not exercise ideological control over access.

Major online platforms increasingly serve the same function. They are the digital roads, mail systems, bulletin boards, and public squares of contemporary society. Their vast network effects make exclusion uniquely severe. A person removed from one dominant platform may not realistically be able to reach friends, customers, voters, readers, or colleagues elsewhere. “Go build your own platform” is not a meaningful answer when the necessary audience, infrastructure, payment access, app distribution, cloud hosting, and search visibility are all controlled by a handful of firms that can coordinate exclusion.

Critics argue that hate-group speech can cause social harm and that platforms have a responsibility to protect vulnerable people. The concern is serious. Forcing hateful ideas into the open can also expose them to scrutiny, rebuttal, ridicule, documentation, and public accountability. Driving such movements into hidden channels does not necessarily eliminate them; it may instead make them harder to monitor and challenge.

Moreover, the alternative—a system in which corporations decide what ideas are too dangerous for public discussion—places extraordinary power in unaccountable hands. Content moderation systems are often opaque, inconsistent, and error-prone. Automated filters routinely misclassify satire, journalism, historical material, human-rights documentation, and minority-language speech. Appeals are limited, explanations are vague, and rules can change overnight. A legal duty to carry lawful content should therefore be paired with clear, neutral standards. The legal obligation should apply primarily to dominant, general-purpose communication infrastructure and essential online services whose power over public participation resembles that of utilities or telecommunications networks. The more indispensable and gatekeeping a service becomes, the stronger its duty of neutrality should be.

A society confident in its values should answer bad ideas with argument, evidence, law enforcement against genuine criminal conduct, and voluntary refusal—not with a demand that private corporations erase lawful voices from the digital public square.

If online communication is to remain genuinely free, the rule must be firm: no person should be excluded from essential digital platforms merely because those in power dislike their lawful views. The Case for a Legal Duty to Host All Legal Content:
Absolute Free Speech and the Common‑Carrier Model

1. Introduction

In the digital age, the public square has migrated to a handful of privately‑owned social‑media platforms. These platforms now serve as the principal venues for political debate, cultural exchange, and the dissemination of ideas. Yet, despite their outsized influence, they operate under a regime that permits them to curate, remove, or de‑platform speech they find objectionable. Critics of this regime argue that, because these venues have become the modern equivalent of the town‑hall, they should be legally compelled to carry all lawful expression—including speech that many find odious, such as that emanating from hate groups. This essay advances the position that such a requirement is both principled and practical, grounded in the doctrine of absolute free speech and the historical legal framework of common‑carrier obligations.

2. The Philosophical Foundation: Absolute Free Speech

2.1 The Marketplace of Ideas

The classic liberal justification for unrestricted speech rests on John Stuart Mill’s “marketplace of ideas.” Mill argued that truth emerges when all ideas—however repugnant—are allowed to compete. Suppressing any idea, even one that appears false or harmful, deprives society of the corrective that counter‑speech provides. If the state (or a private entity) can banish “offensive” speech, it assumes the impossible role of an omniscient arbiter of truth, a role that history shows is prone to abuse.

2.2 The Slippery‑Slope of Content‑Based Regulation

A second philosophical concern is the “slippery‑slope” problem. Once a platform is empowered to remove speech on the basis of “hate,” the criteria for removal become a moving target. What begins as a ban on explicit violent incitement can expand to encompass political dissent, religious criticism, or even humor perceived as insensitive. By mandating that platforms host all legal content, the law creates a bright‑line rule that prevents selective enforcement and the accompanying chilling effect.

3. The Legal Framework: Common‑Carrier Doctrine

3.1 Historical Antecedents

The concept of the common carrier originated in the transportation sector: railroads, telegraphs, and later telephone companies were required to carry all lawful traffic without discrimination. The rationale was that these entities possessed “public‑utility” characteristics—它们提供的是 essential public services, and they possessed bottleneck power that could be leveraged to censor or favor particular speakers. Because they were “public” in function, they were compelled to act as neutral conduits.

3.2 Applying the Carrier Model to Digital Platforms

Contemporary social‑media firms exhibit precisely the features that triggered common‑carrier obligations in the analog era:

Feature Historical Common Carrier Modern Platform
Essential public service Transportation of people/goods Access to the digital public square
Bottleneck power Single railway line, local telephone switchboard Dominant platforms (e.g., Facebook, X, YouTube)
Neutral infrastructure No interest in the content being carried Intermediary role (hosting, not publishing)
Economic regulation Rate‑setting, non‑discrimination duties Potential liability shields (Section 230)

Because these platforms have become indispensable conduits for speech, they can be analogized to “information carriers.” If the law treats them as common carriers, they would be obligated to transmit any lawful content, absent a legitimate, content‑neutral reason for exclusion (e.g., incitement to imminent lawless action, child sexual abuse material, or genuine threats).

4. Arguments for a Legal Duty to Host

4.1 Preventing Private Censorship

When a handful of corporations decide what can be said online, the result is a de‑facto censorship apparatus that is insulated from democratic accountability. By imposing a duty to host, the state ensures that the “public” space remains pluralistic, rather than being ruled by the ideological preferences of a corporate board.

4.2 Preserving the “Public Forum” Doctrine

Courts have long recognized that the government cannot discriminate against speech in a traditional public forum (e.g., streets and parks). The digital analog—the large‑scale social‑media platform—should be treated similarly. A legal requirement to host all lawful content would extend the public‑forum principle to the medium where most modern discourse occurs.

4.3 Encouraging Counter‑Speech, Not Suppression

When hate speech is removed, the speakers often retreat to fringe echo chambers where their views are reinforced without external challenge. By forcing platforms to host such speech, society retains the opportunity to confront it with counter‑speech, education, and alternative narratives—far more effective tools than outright deletion.

4.4 Fostering Technological Neutrality

A neutral hosting rule would prevent platforms from manipulating algorithmic amplification or demotion based on political viewpoint. Such neutrality is essential for preserving the integrity of the information ecosystem and for ensuring that the public can assess ideas on their merits, not on the basis of hidden corporate preferences.

5. Practical Considerations

5.1 Liability and Safe‑Harbor Provisions

The common‑carrier model can be reconciled with existing liability frameworks (e.g., Section 230 in the United States). Under a carrier regime, platforms would retain safe‑harbor protections for user‑generated content while being required to carry it. The law would impose a duty of non‑discrimination, not a duty to endorse or amplify any particular message.

5.2 Enforcement Mechanisms

Regulatory bodies could oversee compliance through periodic audits, complaint mechanisms, and penalties for systematic de‑platforming of lawful content. Such oversight mirrors the public‑utility commissions that monitor traditional carriers, ensuring transparency and accountability.

5.3 Balancing Competing Interests

While the duty to host would be broad, it is not absolute. The law can still carve out narrow categories—incitement to imminent violence, harassment that crosses into true threats, and illegal content—that are legitimately excluded under the “clear and present danger” test. The key is that any exclusion must be content‑neutral and narrowly tailored.

6. Conclusion

The digital public square is no longer a place where the state controls the podium; it is a network of privately owned, yet socially essential, platforms. To preserve the democratic functions of free expression, the law must step in and treat these entities as what they have effectively become: common carriers of information. By mandating that they host all lawful speech—including the most controversial viewpoints espoused by hate groups—we honor the philosophical imperative of absolute free speech, prevent the concentration of private censorship power, and uphold the historic principle that bottlenecks of communication must remain neutral conduits. In doing so, society retains the ability to confront ideas it despises, rather than burying them in the shadows of algorithmic suppression. The legal duty to host is thus both a safeguard for the free exchange of ideas and a practical application of the common‑carrier model to the modern information highway.

Title: The Imperative of Absolute Free Speech Online: Why Platforms Must Be Legally Bound as Common Carriers

In an era where digital platforms have become the public squares of the 21st century, the question of who controls speech — and who may silence it — has never been more urgent. While many advocate for the censorship of so-called “hate speech” in the name of civility or safety, this essay argues unflinchingly that social media platforms and online services must be legally required to host all legal content, including speech from groups widely deemed offensive or hateful. This mandate must be grounded in two foundational pillars: the principle of absolute free speech, as envisioned by classical liberal thought and the First Amendment, and the legal doctrine of common carrier obligations, which compels essential infrastructure providers to serve all comers without discrimination.

I. Absolute Free Speech: The Bedrock of a Free Society

The right to free speech is not granted to protect popular, polite, or politically correct opinions. It exists — and must be defended most vigorously — precisely for the speech we despise. As Justice Louis Brandeis wrote in Whitney v. California (1927), “If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil by the processes of education, the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence.”

Banning “hate speech” — a term so nebulous and subjective that it often includes political dissent, historical revisionism, and unpopular religious views — invites arbitrariness and authoritarian drift. Who defines “hate”? Today’s marginalized minority might be tomorrow’s censored heretic. In the United States, the First Amendment does not carve out exceptions for “hateful” speech unless it meets the narrow Brandenburg standard: speech that is intended and likely to incite imminent lawless action. Outside that tiny exception, all speech is protected — and rightly so.

Social media platforms, by suppressing legal speech under vague community guidelines, have become de facto arbiters of ideological orthodoxy. When Twitter bans a Holocaust denier, or Facebook removes a post quoting Thomas Jefferson out of context, they do not protect society — they infantilize it. They assume citizens cannot be trusted to confront repugnant ideas, evaluate them, and reject them through reason. This is not enlightenment; it is paternalism masquerading as virtue.

II. Common Carrier Obligations: Restoring Neutrality to Digital Infrastructure

Social media platforms are no longer mere private companies offering optional services. They are the railroads, telegraphs, and telephone networks of our digital age — essential conduits for public discourse, commerce, education, and political mobilization. As such, they must be regulated under common carrier principles, which have long governed utilities and infrastructure providers in Western legal systems.

Under common carrier law, entities that provide a general service to the public are prohibited from discriminating among users or content. A telephone company cannot refuse to connect a call because it dislikes the caller’s politics. A railway cannot deny passage to someone based on their creed. Similarly, if Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter are indispensable for modern civic life — which they demonstrably are — they must be barred from editorializing, shadow-banning, or demonetizing users based on viewpoint.

Legally compelling these platforms to host all legal content does not equate to endorsing that content. It simply recognizes that the power to exclude is too great to be left in the hands of unaccountable corporate executives or algorithmic black boxes. Common carrier status would restore neutrality, transparency, and due process to digital public squares.

III. The Slippery Slope of Selective Censorship

Once platforms are allowed to ban “hate groups,” the definition inevitably expands. The Southern Poverty Law Center labels mainstream conservative organizations as “hate groups.” The EU criminalizes “denigration” of religion. Canada prosecutes dissenters for “misinformation.” When private platforms adopt government-aligned definitions of permissible speech, they become instruments of state censorship — whether formally or informally.

Moreover, banning “hate groups” does not eradicate their ideas — it drives them underground, where they fester in encrypted forums and radicalize without counterargument. Open sunlight is the best disinfectant. Allowing neo-Nazis to tweet exposes their absurdity and moral bankruptcy to millions. Banning them grants them martyrdom and mystery. History shows that censorship fuels extremism; open debate defuses it.

Even the most vile speech must be tolerated because the alternative — state-sanctioned or corporate-sanctioned speech control — is infinitely more dangerous. The power to ban “hate” speech is the power to ban any unpopular idea. Conservatives fear being silenced today for defending biological reality or traditional values; progressives may find themselves silenced tomorrow for advocating wealth redistribution or police abolition. The weaponized moderation we tolerate now will be turned against us all.

IV. Practical Implementation and Counterarguments

Critics will claim that forcing platforms to host all legal speech will make them unusable cesspools of toxicity. This is defeatist and empirically false. Platforms can still offer robust user-controlled filtering — allowing individuals to hide, mute, or block content they find offensive — without denying the speech’s existence on the platform. Reddit and 4chan, despite minimal moderation, have not collapsed into incoherence. Users adapt.

Others argue that platforms have a right to curate content as “publishers.” But publishers select content; platforms host it. Facebook does not write your posts. YouTube does not script your videos. Their function is distribution — not editorial judgment. To claim publisher status when convenient, and infrastructure status when profitable, is a legal and moral fraud.

Finally, objectors will cite international laws or corporate responsibility. But no corporation’s “values” outweigh a civilization’s commitment to open discourse. And no international treaty should override the foundational right to free expression in sovereign nations like the United States. If German law bans Holocaust denial, let German courts prosecute violators — but do not compel American platforms to become global speech police.

Conclusion: The Courage to Tolerate the Intolerable

A free society is not measured by how it treats the popular and agreeable, but by how it defends the despised and detestable. To surrender the principle of absolute free speech online is to surrender the soul of liberal democracy. Social media platforms, as the new public infrastructure of global discourse, must be legally bound to host all legal speech — without exception, without apology.

This is not a defense of hate. It is a defense of liberty. It is not naivety — it is courage. Courage to believe that truth will prevail in open combat with falsehood. Courage to trust citizens to navigate complexity without corporate nannyism. Courage to uphold the radical, indispensable principle that the remedy for bad speech is more speech — never silence.

Enshrine common carrier obligations. Protect absolute free speech. Demand that platforms carry all legal content — especially the ugly, the offensive, the unthinkable. For if we will not defend the speech we hate, we do not believe in free speech at all.

— END —

────────────────────────────── Title: Defending Unfettered Expression: The Case for Legally Requiring Social Media Platforms to Host All Legal Content

In an era where information flows instantaneously around the globe, social media platforms and online services have become the digital public square. This transformation has engendered a pressing question: Should these private entities, which have assumed roles analogous to traditional public utilities, be legally mandated to host all legal content—even speech that many find abhorrent, including that from hate groups? This essay argues that the answer is yes. The case rests on two pillars: the absolute nature of free speech and the common carrier obligations that should now extend to digital intermediaries.

I. Absolute Free Speech as the Ultimate Value

At its core, absolute free speech is not merely an abstract ideal—it is a fundamental democratic value. The freedom to express even the most controversial and unpopular opinions is central to maintaining an environment where ideas can be debated openly. To deny any legal speech, however repugnant it might seem, is to weaken the very foundation of a liberal democracy. Historically, the protection of free speech has always been most vigorously defended when the views in question are extreme or unpopular. The rationale is simple: if society shields even its most offensive ideas from censorship, then it creates an atmosphere where open inquiry and critical discussion are prioritized over suppression and dogma.

Critics argue that hate speech can incite violence or perpetuate harm against vulnerable groups. However, the answer should never be to restrict speech proactively, but rather to rely on robust counter-speech, public debate, and, where necessary, law enforcement action against criminal behavior. Allowing offensive ideas to be aired rather than censored provides an opportunity for their counterargument and exposes such ideologies to public scrutiny. Silencing these ideas is a dangerous path toward authoritarianism, wherein subjective judgments about what constitutes “acceptable” speech give way to arbitrary censorship.

II. Social Media Platforms as the Modern Public Square

Social media platforms are not isolated enclaves—they have replaced traditional news outlets, public forums, and even aspects of the interpersonal public sphere. In many countries, for a significant portion of the population, platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube are where political debates take place, opinions are formed, and individuals encounter a multiplicity of perspectives. By operating as the default mode of public discourse, these platforms shoulder immense responsibilities that were once common to public spaces. Their governance decisions have far-reaching effects on political opinions, social movements, and the health of democratic debate.

If the modern public square is to remain open and inclusive, then these platforms must embrace principles that ensure no lawful viewpoint is excluded from the marketplace of ideas. To do otherwise is to allow private entities to wield unprecedented power over public discourse—as arbiters who decide, based on their own criteria or external pressures, which ideas deserve amplification and which do not. Such discretion poses a genuine risk of political bias and ideological hegemony. Legal obligations to host all legal content would remove the subjective filter imposed by platforms and ensure that there is a level playing field for all viewpoints, irrespective of how distasteful or provocative they may be.

III. The Common Carrier Analogy and Its Implications for Digital Platforms

Historically, common carriers—like telephone companies and postal services—have been legally required to deliver their services impartially and without discrimination. The ethos behind common carrier regulations is straightforward: when an entity’s service or infrastructure is critical for communication, it must not favor one customer or opinion over another. Social media platforms, given their ubiquity and centrality to public discourse, have taken on a role analogous to that of a public utility. When they decide what speech to allow or suppress, they effectively perform the gatekeeping function that governments once held—and that is inherently dangerous.

By invoking the common carrier analogy, we argue that social media companies, if they wish to continue serving as the digital equivalent of a public forum, must be held to a similar standard of nondiscrimination. Just as a highway cannot legally obstruct traffic based on the destination, these platforms should not be permitted to curate content based on its ideological bent. Mandating that all legal content be hosted protects against the consolidation of power in the hands of a few private actors who might otherwise use their platforms to advance narrow interests. Legal enforcement of this principle would ensure that no viewpoint is unjustly marginalized and that the public square remains accessible to all lawful ideas—even those that many might personally reject.

IV. Counterarguments and the Path Forward

Opponents of this view often point to the potential harm that hate speech might inflict on society. They argue that requiring platforms to host such content could lead to increased polarization, discrimination, or even violence. However, it is important to note that the legal requirement would only extend to content that is lawful. Incitement to imminent violence and direct threats would still be subject to existing laws that protect public safety. Moreover, the prohibition of lawfully expressed ideas sets a dangerous precedent; today it is hate speech, and tomorrow it might be dissent or criticism of entrenched power structures.

Additionally, critics suggest that platform moderation is necessary to protect users from harmful content and to preserve the quality of public discourse. While moderation can be necessary, it should be performed in a transparent and accountable manner, ideally guided by the same principles that undergird common carrier obligations. Content should not be excised arbitrarily; instead, any decisions about removal must be made with clear, publicly accountable criteria. Legal mandates can serve as a safeguard against the misuse of discretionary power, ensuring that the decision to remove content is not taken lightly or influenced by extraneous pressures.

V. Conclusion

In conclusion, upholding the principle of absolute free speech is essential for the health of democratic society. Social media platforms and online services have evolved from mere private businesses into vital public arenas, comparable in their role to traditional common carriers. As such, they should be legally mandated to host all legal content, including that from hate groups. Such a requirement is not an endorsement of hateful ideologies; rather, it is a commitment to a society where ideas are met with reasoned debate, counter-speech, and a robust marketplace of ideas. Protecting free speech—even when it is offensive—is a bulwark against authoritarianism and a necessary safeguard for true democratic discourse.

In an era where digital platforms have become the predominant public square, the question of whether these platforms should be legally required to host all legal content is more pertinent than ever. The Principle of Absolute Free Speech

The cornerstone of a free society is the protection of unpopular speech. As the iconic American jurist Louis Brandeis famously argued, the remedy for harmful speech is "more speech, not enforced silence." When we permit platforms to selectively censor even lawful but offensive content, we establish a dangerous precedent where corporate entities determine the boundaries of acceptable discourse. These corporations, driven by profit motives and shareholder interests, have demonstrated repeatedly that they cannot be trusted with the immense responsibility of regulating global speech.

When platforms maintain the authority to determine what speech is permissible, they inevitably become arbiters of political discourse—with profound implications for democracy.

Common Carrier Obligations

The concept of common carriers has historical roots in telecommunications, where companies were required to serve all customers without discrimination. As digital platforms have become essential infrastructure for communication, applying common carrier obligations to these services is both logical and necessary. When platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube control access to hundreds of millions of users, their power to exclude certain voices raises serious concerns about the concentration of communicative power.

The telecommunications model provides a compelling framework: just as telephone companies cannot refuse service to certain callers based on their political views, social media platforms should not be permitted to selectively exclude lawful content. This approach does not prevent platforms from addressing genuinely illegal content such as threats, harassment, or incitement to violence—but it does require them to host lawful speech that they might find objectionable.

The Danger of Slippery Slopes in Content Moderation

Content moderation inevitably follows a slippery slope. What begins as a reasonable policy against explicit harassment can expand to encompass legitimate political dissent. When platforms begin censoring certain types of speech, the scope of moderation tends to grow rather than shrink. This phenomenon is evident in the ever-changing community standards that platforms implement—standards that frequently expand to cover increasingly broad categories of speech.

The selective removal of hate groups' content is particularly concerning. History demonstrates that once authorities gain the power to designate which groups are beyond the pale of acceptable discourse, that power will be expanded to include increasingly mainstream viewpoints.

The fundamental assumption underlying absolute free speech protections is that the marketplace of ideas—with all its flaws—remains the best mechanism for distinguishing truth from falsehood. When speech is suppressed, we lose the opportunity to confront bad ideas with better ones. As John Stuart Mill argued in "On Liberty," even false ideas contain elements of truth that might otherwise be lost in a homogenous discourse.

Should Social Media Platforms Be Required to Host All Legal Speech?

The question of whether social media platforms and online services should be legally required to host all lawful content is one of the central policy debates of the digital age. Supporters argue that large platforms function like essential communications infrastructure and should therefore operate under rules similar to those imposed on common carriers. Opponents respond that private services have rights of editorial discretion, that compelled hosting would undermine safety and usability, and that legality is too weak a standard for governing online spaces used by billions of people. A sound analysis must take both concerns seriously.

The strongest argument in favor of mandatory hosting rules is rooted in the growing importance of major platforms to public discourse. A handful of companies now mediate political communication, news distribution, professional networking, and cultural life at enormous scale. When a platform removes lawful speech, the practical effect can resemble exclusion from a modern public square. From this perspective, concentrated private control over speech creates risks similar to government censorship, even if the legal mechanism is different. Advocates of stronger access rights argue that democratic societies should not allow a small number of corporations to decide which lawful viewpoints may reach mass audiences.

This argument becomes more forceful when framed through the concept of common carriage. Traditionally, common carriers such as railroads, telephones, and certain utilities have been required to serve customers without discriminating based on viewpoint. The logic is that when an entity provides essential transmission services, holds itself out as open to the public, and benefits from network effects or market power, it may be subject to duties of nondiscrimination. Applied to digital platforms, this analogy suggests that dominant services should not selectively exclude legal speech simply because executives or moderators dislike its content. On this view, the role of a platform is to transmit user expression, not to act as a gatekeeper of acceptable opinion.

Supporters also contend that a legality-based standard would be clearer and less arbitrary than current moderation systems. Today, users often face vague rules against “harmful,” “hateful,” or “misleading” content that are enforced inconsistently and sometimes opaquely. Errors are common, appeals are slow, and moderation decisions can appear politically biased even when they are not. Requiring platforms to carry all lawful speech would replace discretionary line-drawing with a more objective baseline. If content is illegal—such as true threats, unlawful harassment, or criminal solicitation—it can be removed. If it is lawful, it stays. Advocates believe such a rule would better protect dissent, minority viewpoints, satire, controversial scholarship, and unpopular political movements.

At the same time, there are serious objections to imposing such a legal duty. The first is that social media platforms are not merely passive conduits. They rank, recommend, amplify, label, and curate content. Their design choices shape what users see and how speech spreads. That makes them unlike a traditional telephone company, which carries communications without arranging them into attention-maximizing feeds. Because platforms are engaged in a kind of editorial organization, critics argue that they should retain discretion over what they host and promote. A law forcing them to carry speech they reject may itself raise freedom-of-expression concerns by compelling private entities to associate with messages they do not endorse.

A second objection is practical: “legal” does not mean harmless. Many forms of speech that remain lawful can still be deeply destructive, including glorification of violence, racist propaganda, coordinated humiliation, and disinformation that exploits moments of crisis. Even when such material falls short of criminality, it can drive users away, intimidate vulnerable communities, and degrade the quality of public discourse. Services used by children, families, schools, and workplaces often need rules stricter than criminal law in order to remain usable. If platforms could remove only illegal content, they might become far more hostile environments, rewarding the most inflammatory actors and making ordinary participation less safe.

There is also a difficulty in deciding which services would qualify for common-carrier treatment. Applying a blanket hosting mandate to every online forum, gaming service, messaging app, and community site would be unworkable and would destroy the diversity of online spaces. A professional networking site, a hobby forum, and a platform for children cannot all sensibly operate under identical speech rules. Narrowing the mandate to only the largest and most dominant platforms might solve part of the problem, but then legislators would need to define market power, interoperability, covered services, and exceptions for specialized communities.

A more balanced approach may be preferable. Rather than forcing platforms to host all lawful content, lawmakers could pursue reforms that address concentrated private power while preserving moderation flexibility. These might include transparency requirements, meaningful notice and appeal systems, clearer rules, due-process protections for users, data portability, interoperability, and restrictions on deceptive or discriminatory enforcement. Governments could also distinguish between hosting and amplification: a platform might be allowed to downrank or label certain lawful content without necessarily banning it outright. Such measures could reduce arbitrary censorship concerns while still allowing services to protect users and maintain functional communities.

In the end, the case for requiring platforms to host all legal speech captures an important truth: private control over digital communication can threaten open debate when exercised arbitrarily or at massive scale. But the strongest counterargument is equally important: online services are not neutral pipes, and a legality-only standard may be too blunt to protect users and sustain healthy forums. The challenge for law and policy is not simply to choose between unrestricted hosting and unrestricted moderation, but to design institutions that preserve freedom, fairness, safety, and pluralism at the same time.

A legal regime that requires social media platforms and major online services to host all lawful content—including the speech of hate groups—is both principled and necessary. It follows from a serious commitment to freedom of expression, from the logic of common carrier obligations, and from the dangers of delegating censorship power to private corporations. If we truly believe in free speech as a foundational value of a liberal, pluralistic society, then we must be prepared to protect speech we detest, not only speech we like.

  1. Free speech as a principle, not a preference
  • A society that values free expression cannot treat it as a fashion accessory—invoked to protect popular or majority viewpoints while quietly abandoned for those that offend, disturb, or disgust.
  • The historical and philosophical core of free speech doctrine is precisely the protection of unpopular, extremist, and hateful views. Popular speech does not need protection; legal protection is meaningful only when it shelters the speech that most people would rather suppress.
  • Allowing only “acceptable” or “responsible” speech is not free speech; it is managed speech. Once the norm is that controversial viewpoints may be erased from major communication channels, the scope of acceptable speech is at the mercy of whoever wields that erasing power.
  • If the law draws a clear boundary between legal and illegal expression, then platforms should be obligated to host what the law permits. Anything else allows corporations to impose a parallel speech code that can be harsher, more arbitrary, and less accountable than democratically enacted standards.
  1. Why common carrier logic fits the modern information infrastructure
  • Social media platforms and dominant online services now function as core infrastructure for public discourse, association, and political life—much like the telephone network, mail service, or basic utilities in earlier eras.
  • We already recognize that essential carriers and utilities have duties of neutrality:
    • Telephone companies cannot cut off service because they disapprove of what people say over the phone, as long as it is legal.
    • The postal service cannot refuse to deliver lawful materials because it finds them offensive.
  • The rationale is simple: when an entity controls critical pathways of communication or commerce, the power to discriminate based on viewpoint or identity becomes too dangerous and distorting for a democratic society to tolerate.
  • Today’s major platforms—global social networks, video platforms, cloud hosts, app stores, payment processors, search engines—wield the same gatekeeping power over speech and association. Their choices, collectively, determine which voices can be heard at scale.
  • Treating them as common carriers for lawful content:
    • Limits arbitrary viewpoint discrimination.
    • Prevents collusive or cascading deplatforming where multiple services simultaneously erase entire political or ideological communities from public visibility.
    • Ensures that speakers’ basic access to the digital public square does not hinge on ideological alignment with a handful of executives, trust-and-safety teams, or activist pressure campaigns.
  1. The danger of privatized censorship
  • Delegating control over speech to private platforms sounds benign to some precisely because it evades constitutional scrutiny. “It’s not the government, so it’s not censorship,” the argument goes.
  • But functionally, viewpoint-based removals on dominant platforms are censorship in everything but formal label. They:
    • Silence speakers at scale.
    • Suppress political and cultural minorities.
    • Shape public opinion by invisibly filtering what can be seen, shared, or debated.
  • Because these decisions are:
    • Made behind closed doors.
    • Influenced by opaque internal policies, PR calculations, advertiser demands, and political pressure.
    • Enforced through algorithmic systems that users cannot meaningfully audit or challenge. they are less accountable than even flawed state regulation.
  • Without a legal obligation to carry all lawful speech:
    • Platforms can and do define “hate,” “harm,” “misinformation,” or “extremism” expansively to capture legitimate dissent and ideological opposition.
    • Advocacy and viewpoints that fall outside emerging elite consensus can be throttled or banned—not because they are illegal, but because they are unfashionable or threatening to institutional interests.
  • A serious commitment to free speech should reject this quiet outsourcing of censorship. If expression is legal, it should not be exiled from the main avenues of communication by private fiat.
  1. Consistency, fairness, and protection for all minorities
  • Many who favor aggressive moderation today do so in the name of protecting vulnerable groups. Their concern is morally serious—but the solution they favor is dangerously shortsighted.
  • Any tool created to silence one set of views can later be used to silence its ideological opponents. History repeatedly shows that censorship mechanisms, once normalized, drift toward suppressing dissidents, whistleblowers, and marginalized perspectives.
  • Mandatory carriage of all lawful content:
    • Protects racial, religious, and sexual minorities whose views might be labeled “radical,” “offensive,” or “destabilizing” by those in power.
    • Protects political minorities, dissidents, and unconventional thinkers from being algorithmically marginalized for contradicting prevailing narratives.
    • Avoids the hypocrisy of a system where each side loves “platform responsibility” when their enemies are silenced, then cries censorship when the pendulum swings.
  • An absolute principle—“if it is legal, it must be allowed”—is intellectually honest, stable over time, and protective across ideological cycles. It prevents one generation’s moral panic from becoming permanent structural exclusion.
  1. The “harm” objection and why it does not justify discretionary silencing

A central objection is that hosting lawful but hateful speech causes real harm: it can foster hostility, radicalization, or fear among targeted communities. This concern must be addressed directly.

  • First, a liberal society already recognizes a boundary: speech that directly crosses into illegality (true threats, incitement, targeted harassment, etc.) can and should be banned. The argument here is about speech that remains legal under those standards.
  • Second, fear of indirect or speculative harm cannot be a license to erase legal speech from the primary channels of communication. If it were:
    • Any speech challenging dominant ideologies could be labeled “harmful” to social cohesion.
    • Critical reporting, controversial academic work, or religious doctrine could be censored on vague “harm” grounds.
  • Third, visibility does not equal endorsement. Requiring platforms to carry lawful content is not mandating support; it is mandating neutrality. We trust citizens to encounter, criticize, and reject bad ideas without needing corporate filters to sanitize reality for them.
  • Fourth, forced suppression can backfire:
    • It feeds martyrdom narratives: “The system is afraid of our ideas.”
    • It drives extremist speech into closed, less visible ecosystems where it is harder to scrutinize, counter, or deter.
  • If hateful or extremist ideas are dangerous, the most durable answer is more speech:
    • Public rebuttal, exposure of falsehoods, rigorous counter-argument.
    • Education and social resilience, not digital erasure.
  • Accepting some discomfort and offense is the price of intellectual autonomy. A society that pathologizes exposure to hateful views as intolerable harm is a society that is, in practice, endorsing paternalistic control over what adults are permitted to hear.
  1. Power, pluralism, and the reality of corporate incentives
  • Large platforms are responsive to:
    • Governments that threaten regulation.
    • Major advertisers that fear controversy.
    • Coordinated activist campaigns that impose reputational costs.

  • Legal must-carry obligations:
    • Strip away the incentive and the excuse for ideologically selective enforcement: “We don’t have a choice; the law requires us to host all legal content.”

  1. User choice instead of corporate control

Requiring platforms to carry all lawful content does not mean every user must see everything, nor does it mean platforms cannot structure the user experience.

A well-designed must-carry framework can and should:

  • Allow:
    • User-level controls (blocking, muting, filters, keyword tools).
    • Opt-in content filtering services (e.g., third-party or community-based moderation layers) that users can choose according to their values.
    • Ranking algorithms oriented to user preferences without deleting lawful speech from existence.
  • Prohibit:
    • Viewpoint-based bans and removals of lawful content from the platform itself.
    • Coordinated exclusion of lawful speakers from essential infrastructure (hosting, payments, app stores) purely for their views.
  • This shifts power:
    • Away from centralized moderation bureaucracies.
    • Toward individual autonomy and diverse community norms.
  • The principle: everything legal can exist and be reachable; individuals and communities decide what they engage with. That is what a mature free speech culture looks like.
  1. Democratic legitimacy and clarity
  • When platforms enforce speech codes stricter than the law, we end up with two parallel systems:
    • The democratically enacted legal standard of what citizens may say.
    • The privately decreed corporate standard of what they may say in practice.
  • This dual system:
    • Undermines democratic decision-making, because the practical boundary of available speech is set by unaccountable firms.
    • Confuses citizens, who no longer know which rules govern them and have no meaningful recourse when they are digitally erased.
  • A legal must-carry rule aligns practice with principle:
    • If society, through democratic processes, decides certain speech is intolerable, it can criminalize it under clear, reviewable standards; then platforms can, indeed must, remove it.
    • If society does not criminalize it, platforms may not silently nullify that democratic choice.
  • Such clarity:
    • Forces any restriction on expression into the open, subject to public debate, legislative scrutiny, and judicial review.
    • Eliminates the convenience of “censorship by proxy,” where governments pressure platforms to do informally what they cannot do constitutionally.
  1. The absolute principle as a safeguard for the future

The question is not whether you are comfortable with platforms hosting the speech you consider hateful now. The question is whether you are comfortable giving today’s platforms—and tomorrow’s—unfettered authority to decide which opinions, movements, religions, or identities may appear in the central channels of communication.

An absolute, law-based standard—host all legal content—is the only robust safeguard against that authority being abused.

It:

  • Defends the most unpopular and reviled speech, thereby defending everyone’s speech.
  • Respects citizens as moral agents capable of confronting bad ideas.
  • Constrains powerful corporations and prevents them from functioning as unelected censors.
  • Reinforces democratic legitimacy by aligning speech norms with public law, not private whim.
  • Preserves a genuinely pluralistic digital public sphere where conflicting ideologies coexist and contend openly.

If we are serious about free speech as a foundational value rather than a rhetorical tactic, then we must accept its hard implications. That means legally requiring the dominant platforms and essential online services of our era to carry all lawful expression—including that of hate groups. The alternative is a future in which the boundaries of public thought are silently drawn by those who own the servers, not by the people who live under the laws.
